# Legal Frameworks for AI: GDPR and the EU AI Act

## When the Law Knocked on the Door

It's 3 a.m. when the legal team at a mid-sized HR tech startup receives the email. Subject line: "Formal complaint pursuant to Art. 77 GDPR." A job applicant—call her Maria—has filed with the data protection authority. She wants to know why the company's AI screening tool rejected her application in forty-seven seconds. She wants the logic behind the decision. She wants the training data. She wants accountability.

The startup's CEO thought they'd done everything right. They used publicly available LinkedIn profiles. They optimized for "efficiency." They reduced time-to-hire by 60%. They never asked for consent because, well, the data was already public. Besides, AI makes *objective* decisions—no human bias, no discrimination, just pure mathematics.

**Three weeks later, the fine arrives: €250,000.**

Not because the algorithm discriminated (though it probably did). Not because they violated employment law (though that investigation is ongoing). But because they fundamentally misunderstood what "personal data" means, what "lawfulness" requires, and what rights individuals possess when machines make consequential decisions about their lives.

Maria's case isn't hypothetical. Variants of this scenario play out across Europe daily as organizations discover that AI systems processing personal data operate within one of the world's strictest regulatory frameworks—and that ignorance provides no defense.

---

## Why Legal Frameworks Matter

You might think: "I'm developing technology, not practicing law." Or: "Compliance is someone else's problem." Both perspectives are dangerously incomplete.

Legal frameworks don't merely constrain what you can build—they define what you *should* build. The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and the EU AI Act aren't bureaucratic obstacles to innovation. They're attempts to answer fundamental questions: Who controls personal information? Who bears responsibility when algorithms cause harm? Under what conditions should certain technologies simply not exist?

These regulations emerged from decades of abuse. From discriminatory profiling. From opaque surveillance. From the realization that technology amplifies power imbalances—and that without legal boundaries, those imbalances become permanent.

Computer scientist Kate Crawford argues that "AI is neither artificial nor intelligent." It's human labor, extracted data, and infrastructural power wrapped in mathematical formalism. Legal frameworks force us to acknowledge that reality.

---

## What You'll Learn in This Module

This module unpacks two cornerstone regulations governing AI in the European Union. You'll understand the **principles** underlying data protection law, the **requirements** for deploying high-risk AI systems, and the **prohibitions** against certain practices deemed fundamentally incompatible with human rights.

You'll learn to:
- Identify when AI systems trigger GDPR obligations and which legal bases apply
- Recognize prohibited AI practices under the AI Act
- Analyze high-risk classification and associated compliance requirements
- Navigate the tension between automated efficiency and individual rights
- Apply legal reasoning to ambiguous cases involving emerging technologies

This isn't about memorizing articles. It's about developing legal literacy as a professional competency.

---

## Part 1: The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR)

### The Foundation: Personal Data as a Fundamental Right

The GDPR rests on a premise foreign to many legal traditions: privacy isn't merely a preference or a commercial transaction. It's a **fundamental right** enshrined in the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights (Article 8). You don't trade it away by using a service. Companies don't acquire it by collecting your data.

This philosophical foundation shapes everything that follows.

::: {.flip-card}
#### Personal Data

Any information relating to an **identified or identifiable natural person** ("data subject"). This includes direct identifiers (names, ID numbers), location data, online identifiers (IP addresses, cookies), and any data that—combined with other information—could identify someone.
:::

The definition is deliberately expansive. A photo? Personal data. A voice recording? Personal data. Metadata showing which websites someone visited? Personal data. Biometric templates extracted from facial scans? Absolutely personal data.

**Why does this matter for AI?** Machine learning systems consume vast quantities of data. Training a facial recognition model requires millions of images—each one personal data if it depicts an identifiable person. Building a recruitment algorithm means processing CVs, performance reviews, communication patterns. Every data point potentially triggers GDPR obligations.

The common misconception: "Public data is exempt from GDPR." **False.** Publicly accessible data (social media posts, professional profiles, government records) remains personal data. Collection and processing still require a legal basis.

::: {.details}
#### Processing: Broader Than You Think

Art. 4(2) GDPR defines "processing" as any operation performed on personal data: collection, recording, organization, structuring, storage, adaptation, retrieval, consultation, use, disclosure, dissemination, erasure, or destruction.

**Critical implication:** Even *reading* personal data constitutes processing. Uploading a dataset to your development environment? Processing. Running inference on user inputs? Processing. Storing model outputs? Processing.

You can't avoid GDPR by claiming you're "just training a model" or "only analyzing aggregated data." If personal data enters the pipeline anywhere, GDPR applies.
:::

### The Actors: Controllers and Processors

The GDPR assigns responsibilities based on **functional roles**, not organizational structure.

::: {.flip-card}
#### Controller

The entity that determines the **purposes** and **means** of processing. Controllers decide *why* data is processed and *how* it happens.
:::

::: {.flip-card}
#### Processor

The entity that processes personal data **on behalf of the controller**. Processors follow instructions; they don't determine purposes.
:::

In AI development, identifying your role matters enormously. If you're building a custom recruitment algorithm and deciding which candidate attributes to analyze, you're functioning as a **controller**—even if you're technically a vendor. That means you bear primary legal responsibility.

Cloud providers (AWS, Azure, Google Cloud) typically operate as **processors** when you use their infrastructure. But if you use their pre-trained AI models, the analysis becomes complex. Who decided what attributes the model predicts? Who selected the training data? Shared responsibility models require careful contractual definition.

### The Six Principles: Art. 5 GDPR

Every AI system processing personal data must comply with these foundational principles. They're not suggestions. They're binding legal requirements.

**Principle 1: Lawfulness, Fairness, and Transparency**

Data must be processed legally (meaning: with a valid legal basis under Art. 6). "Fairness" prohibits processing in ways contrary to reasonable expectations. "Transparency" requires clear, accessible information about what you're doing with personal data.

For AI: You cannot deploy a facial recognition system in a public space without informing people. You cannot scrape data from platforms in violation of their terms of service and call it "lawful." You cannot hide algorithmic decision-making behind trade secrecy claims while demanding individuals trust the outcomes.

**Principle 2: Purpose Limitation**

Data collected for one purpose cannot be repurposed for an incompatible second use. If you collected employee performance data to administer payroll, you cannot later use that same data to train a predictive termination model—unless the purposes are compatible or you obtain new consent.

**Critical for AI:** Many machine learning applications involve purpose creep. Data gathered for service provision becomes training data for new products. GDPR demands you assess compatibility *before* repurposing.

**Principle 3: Data Minimization**

Process only data **strictly necessary** for your specified purpose. "As much as necessary, not as much as possible."

This principle directly challenges standard ML practice. Bigger datasets don't automatically mean better models if the additional data isn't necessary. Training on sensitive attributes (race, religion, health status) when those attributes aren't relevant to the legitimate purpose violates data minimization—even if including them marginally improves accuracy.

**Principle 4: Accuracy**

Personal data must be accurate and kept up to date. Inaccurate data must be erased or rectified.

For predictive systems: If your model generates predictions (credit scores, recidivism risk, employee performance ratings), those predictions must be based on accurate inputs. More fundamentally: is a *prediction* about future behavior ever "accurate"? Courts are grappling with this question.

**Principle 5: Storage Limitation**

Data must be deleted when no longer needed for the original purpose.

AI systems often retain training data indefinitely. GDPR demands justification for retention periods. If you trained a model five years ago, can you still justify keeping the training data? Probably not—unless you have a legitimate, documented reason.

**Principle 6: Integrity and Confidentiality**

Implement appropriate security measures to protect against unauthorized access, loss, or damage.

For AI: This means securing training datasets, protecting model weights from extraction attacks, preventing adversarial manipulation, and ensuring deployed systems can't be exploited to leak training data.

::: {.details}
#### Accountability: Proving Compliance

Art. 5(2) GDPR imposes a meta-obligation: The controller must demonstrate compliance with all principles. "Accountability" means you can't merely assert compliance—you must document it.

**Practical implications:**
- Maintain records of processing activities (Art. 30)
- Conduct Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs) for high-risk processing (Art. 35)
- Implement technical and organizational measures demonstrating compliance ("privacy by design")
- Appoint a Data Protection Officer if required (Art. 37-39)

For AI projects: Before deploying a system, document which principles apply, how you've satisfied them, and what safeguards you've implemented. If you can't produce this documentation when regulators ask, you're non-compliant by definition.
:::

### The Legal Bases: Art. 6 GDPR

Processing personal data is **prohibited by default**. You need affirmative legal authorization. Art. 6 provides six possible bases.

::: {.flip-card}
#### Consent (Art. 6(1)(a))

Freely given, specific, informed, and unambiguous indication of the data subject's agreement. Consent must be granular (separate consent for separate purposes) and revocable.
:::

**Why consent is problematic for AI:** Meaningful consent requires understanding what you're consenting to. How do you obtain informed consent for processing involving complex ML pipelines where even developers can't fully explain model behavior? How "free" is consent when refusing means being excluded from essential services?

Consent works for clear, bounded purposes ("We'll use your photo for your employee badge"). It fails for open-ended AI development ("We'll use your data to improve our models in unspecified ways").

::: {.flip-card}
#### Contractual Necessity (Art. 6(1)(b))

Processing necessary to fulfill a contract with the data subject. Example: Processing shipping addresses to deliver purchased goods.
:::

**For AI:** Be cautious claiming contractual necessity. If users can receive the service without the AI processing, it's not "necessary." You can't make AI processing "necessary" by simply writing it into your terms of service if the core service doesn't require it.

::: {.flip-card}
#### Legitimate Interest (Art. 6(1)(f))

Processing necessary for legitimate interests pursued by the controller, **except** where those interests are overridden by the data subject's fundamental rights and freedoms.
:::

This requires a **balancing test**: Your legitimate interest versus individual rights. You must document this balancing.

**Example:** A company has a legitimate interest in preventing fraud. But deploying facial recognition to monitor all employees continuously? The privacy intrusion likely outweighs the interest.

Legitimate interest provides flexibility but demands careful justification. It's not a catch-all for "whatever we want to do."

::: {.case-study}
#### Case: The Recruitment Algorithm

You're developing an AI system to screen job applications for a large corporation. The system analyzes CVs, social media profiles, and publicly available professional information to predict "job fit."

**Question:** Which legal basis applies?

::: {.solution}
**Analysis:**

**Consent** is impractical. Job applicants have unequal bargaining power—refusing consent likely means automatic rejection. Art. 6(1)(a) requires consent be "freely given." When there's a significant power imbalance, consent isn't valid.

**Contractual necessity** doesn't apply. There's no contract yet—this is pre-contractual evaluation. More fundamentally, AI screening isn't *necessary* to evaluate applications (companies managed hiring for centuries without algorithmic pre-screening).

**Legitimate interest** (Art. 6(1)(f)) is the most plausible basis. The employer has a legitimate interest in efficient hiring. But you must balance this against applicants' rights:

- **Transparency:** Inform applicants that AI screening occurs, what data is analyzed, and what consequences follow.
- **Fairness:** Ensure the system doesn't introduce discriminatory bias (which would violate both GDPR's fairness principle and employment discrimination law).
- **Necessity:** Can you achieve the same purpose with less invasive means? If yes, legitimate interest fails.
- **Safeguards:** Implement human review of algorithmic decisions (required by Art. 22, discussed below).

**Conclusion:** Legitimate interest *might* apply if the system includes robust transparency, non-discrimination safeguards, and human oversight. But the legal ground is contestable. A data protection authority reviewing this use case would scrutinize whether the efficiency gains genuinely justify the privacy intrusion—and many would conclude they don't.
:::
:::

### Special Categories: Art. 9 GDPR

Certain data is considered so sensitive that processing is **prohibited by default** with limited exceptions.

**Special category data includes:** racial/ethnic origin, political opinions, religious beliefs, trade union membership, genetic data, biometric data (when processed to uniquely identify someone), health data, and data concerning sex life or sexual orientation.

::: {.details}
#### Why Biometric Data Receives Special Protection

Biometric data (fingerprints, facial templates, voiceprints, iris scans) uniquely identifies individuals based on biological characteristics. Unlike passwords, you can't change your face or fingerprint if they're compromised.

**Art. 9(1) GDPR:** Processing biometric data for unique identification is prohibited unless an exception applies.

**Exceptions include (Art. 9(2)):**
- Explicit consent (higher threshold than regular consent)
- Necessary for employment/social security law (with appropriate safeguards)
- Necessary to protect vital interests when the person is incapable of consent
- Substantial public interest basis under EU/Member State law

**For AI developers:** You cannot train facial recognition systems on scraped photos and claim a legitimate interest. You need explicit consent from individuals whose faces appear in your training data—or another Art. 9(2) exception. "Publicly available photos" doesn't constitute consent for biometric processing.
:::

**The predictive privacy problem:** AI can infer sensitive attributes from non-sensitive data. A model trained on purchase history might predict religious affiliation. A system analyzing writing style might infer mental health conditions. Even if you never directly collect "special category data," you might be *generating* it through inference—and courts are beginning to recognize this as triggering Art. 9 protection.

### Automated Decision-Making: Art. 22 GDPR

This is the provision most directly relevant to AI deployment.

**Art. 22(1):** "The data subject shall have the right not to be subject to a decision based **solely** on automated processing, including profiling, which produces **legal effects** concerning them or **similarly significantly affects** them."

Break this down:

::: {.flip-card}
#### Solely Automated

No meaningful human involvement in the decision. If a human rubber-stamps algorithmic outputs without genuine review, it's still "solely automated."
:::

::: {.flip-card}
#### Legal Effects or Similarly Significant

Examples: Automatic credit denial, algorithmic hiring/firing decisions, insurance pricing, access to essential services. "Significant" is broadly interpreted—anything substantially affecting someone's circumstances qualifies.
:::

::: {.flip-card}
#### Profiling (Art. 4(4))

Automated processing of personal data to evaluate personal aspects, particularly to analyze or predict performance, economic situation, health, preferences, interests, reliability, behavior, location, or movements.
:::

**Key implication:** Individuals have the right to **opt out** of solely automated decisions with significant effects. They can demand human review.

**Exceptions (Art. 22(2)):** Solely automated decisions are permissible if:
- Necessary for contract performance
- Authorized by EU/Member State law with appropriate safeguards
- Based on explicit consent

Even when exceptions apply, **Art. 22(3)** requires implementing safeguards: "the right to obtain human intervention, to express their point of view, and to contest the decision."

::: {.case-study}
#### Case: The Automated Rejection

Sarah (from the ethics module) applies for a social work position. An AI system scans her CV, detects an employment gap and part-time work history, and automatically rejects her application without human review.

**Legal analysis under Art. 22:**

1. **Solely automated?** Yes—no human reviewed her application.
2. **Legal/significant effects?** Yes—job rejection significantly affects her economic situation.
3. **Permissible exception?** 
   - Not contractual necessity (no contract exists).
   - Not based on consent.
   - Not authorized by law with safeguards.

**Conclusion:** This violates Art. 22(1). Sarah has the right to demand human review and to express her perspective. The employer must implement meaningful human oversight—not just a cursory glance at algorithmic outputs, but substantive evaluation where the human can override the algorithm.

**Remedies available to Sarah:**
- File a complaint with the supervisory authority (Art. 77)
- Demand access to information about the automated decision-making logic (Art. 13-15)
- Seek judicial remedy (Art. 79)
- Claim compensation for material/non-material damage (Art. 82)

**Potential consequences for the employer:**
- Administrative fines up to €20 million or 4% of global annual turnover, whichever is higher (Art. 83)
- Corrective measures: Ban on processing, deletion of data
- Reputational damage
- Individual compensation claims
:::

### Transparency Rights: Art. 13-15 GDPR

When processing personal data, controllers must provide specific information to data subjects.

**If data is collected directly from the individual (Art. 13):**
- Identity and contact details of the controller
- Purposes and legal basis for processing
- Recipients of the data
- Retention periods
- Right to access, rectification, erasure, restriction, objection
- Right to withdraw consent (if consent is the legal basis)
- Right to lodge a complaint with supervisory authority
- **If automated decision-making occurs:** Meaningful information about the logic involved, significance, and envisaged consequences

**If data is obtained from other sources (Art. 14):** Similar information, plus the source of the data and which categories were obtained.

**For AI systems:** "Meaningful information about the logic involved" creates tension. Trade secrecy protects algorithmic details. But GDPR prioritizes individual rights over commercial interests. You must disclose enough for people to understand and challenge decisions—even if that reveals some algorithmic logic.

The European Court of Justice has held that transparency obligations cannot be circumvised by invoking trade secrets (Case C-434/16, Nowak).

## Part 2: The EU AI Act

### A New Regulatory Paradigm

On August 1, 2024, the EU AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689) entered into force—the world's first comprehensive legal framework specifically targeting artificial intelligence. Unlike GDPR (which regulates data processing), the AI Act regulates AI **systems** based on their risk to fundamental rights and safety.

**Why a separate regulation?** AI poses risks beyond privacy. Discriminatory algorithms violate equality rights. Manipulative systems undermine autonomy. Opaque high-stakes decision-making threatens due process. The AI Act addresses these harms directly.

::: {.flip-card}
#### AI System (Art. 3(1))

A machine-based system that is designed to operate with varying levels of autonomy and that may exhibit adaptiveness after deployment and that, for explicit or implicit objectives, **infers**, from the input it receives, how to generate outputs such as predictions, content, recommendations, or decisions that can influence physical or virtual environments.
:::

**Key element:** "Infers" distinguishes AI from traditional software. Rule-based systems (if-then logic) aren't AI under this definition. Machine learning models that derive patterns from data *are* AI.

::: {.details}
#### What "Inference" Means

Traditional software executes pre-programmed rules: IF (temperature > 30°C) THEN (activate cooling). No inference—just conditional logic.

AI systems derive models from data. A machine learning model doesn't contain explicit rules for recognizing cats in images. Instead, it *infers* statistical patterns from training examples, then generalizes to new inputs.

**This distinction matters because:**
- Traditional software behavior is fully specified by developers
- AI system behavior *emerges* from training data and learning algorithms
- Emergent behavior creates unpredictability—hence regulatory concern

**Borderline cases:** An algorithm that uses manually crafted decision trees (not learned from data) likely isn't "AI" under the Act. A hybrid system combining rules with learned components would qualify as AI if inference plays a substantial role.
:::

### The Risk-Based Framework

The AI Act classifies systems into four tiers based on risk to fundamental rights, health, and safety.

**Tier 1: Unacceptable Risk → Prohibited**

Certain AI practices are banned outright (Art. 5). No amount of safeguards makes them permissible.

**Tier 2: High Risk → Strict Requirements**

AI systems listed in Annex III or that are safety components of regulated products face mandatory obligations before market placement (Art. 6-15).

**Tier 3: Limited Risk → Transparency Obligations**

Systems interacting with humans (chatbots), generating synthetic content (deepfakes), or used for emotion/biometric categorization must disclose their AI nature (Art. 50).

**Tier 4: Minimal Risk → No Specific Obligations**

AI in video games, spam filters, and similar applications face no additional regulation under the Act.

### Prohibited Practices: Art. 5

These are the "red lines"—AI applications considered fundamentally incompatible with EU values.

**Art. 5(1)(a): Manipulative Techniques**

Deploying subliminal techniques, manipulative techniques, or deceptive techniques that materially distort behavior in a manner that causes or is reasonably likely to cause significant harm.

**Example:** AI systems that exploit psychological vulnerabilities (children, people with disabilities, economic hardship) to manipulate behavior in harmful ways. Think: predatory lending apps using dark patterns optimized by reinforcement learning to maximize user debt.

**Art. 5(1)(b): Exploitation of Vulnerabilities**

Deploying AI to exploit vulnerabilities of specific groups (age, disability, social/economic situation) causing or likely to cause significant harm.

**Art. 5(1)(c): Social Scoring**

Evaluating or classifying individuals or groups based on social behavior or personality traits, with evaluations used for detrimental treatment in contexts **unrelated** to where the data was generated.

::: {.details}
#### What Social Scoring Means

Social scoring assigns scores reflecting trustworthiness, reliability, or "citizenship" based on behavior across multiple contexts.

**Classic example:** China's Social Credit System, which penalizes citizens for behaviors ranging from traffic violations to online speech, affecting access to employment, education, travel.

**What's prohibited:** Using someone's social media activity to determine creditworthiness. Rating employees based on personal activities outside work. Aggregating behavioral data across unrelated contexts to classify people as "high risk."

**What remains permissible:** Credit scoring based on financial history (directly related context). Performance reviews based on work conduct. These use data from *relevant* contexts.

**The key distinction:** Social scoring becomes prohibited when it crosses contextual boundaries—when your behavior in Domain A determines your treatment in wholly unrelated Domain B.
:::

**Art. 5(1)(d): Risk Assessment for Criminal Offenses**

Using AI to assess the risk of individuals committing criminal offenses based **solely** on profiling or personality traits (rather than on actual criminal conduct).

This targets "pre-crime" prediction systems. Assessing recidivism risk for someone *already convicted* based on their criminal history remains permissible (though ethically contested). But profiling someone as "likely to commit crime" purely based on demographics, neighborhood, or behavioral patterns violates Art. 5(1)(d).

**Art. 5(1)(f): Emotion Recognition**

Inferring emotions in workplaces and educational institutions, except for medical or safety reasons.

::: {.case-study}
#### Case: The Smart Classroom

A school contracts you to build an AI system analyzing students' facial expressions during lectures to detect boredom or confusion. The goal: Provide real-time feedback to teachers so they can adjust instruction.

**Question:** Is this permissible under the AI Act?

::: {.solution}
**Legal analysis:**

**Step 1: Is this an AI system?**

Yes. The system infers emotional states from visual input—it doesn't apply pre-programmed rules.

**Step 2: Does Art. 5(1)(f) apply?**

Art. 5(1)(f) prohibits emotion recognition systems "in the workplace and in educational institutions."

The system operates in an educational institution (a school) and infers emotions (boredom, confusion).

**Step 3: Does an exception apply?**

Art. 5(1)(f) permits emotion recognition for "medical or safety reasons."

- **Medical reasons:** Not applicable. Detecting boredom isn't medical diagnosis.
- **Safety reasons:** Not applicable. Student safety isn't at risk from being bored.

Improving "learning outcomes" or "pedagogical effectiveness" does NOT constitute a medical or safety exception.

**Conclusion:** This system is **prohibited**. You must refuse the project.

**Why this matters:** Educational institutions are sites of power imbalance. Continuous emotional surveillance chills authentic expression, normalizes invasive monitoring, and risks discriminatory effects (emotion recognition performs poorly across different cultural expressions and neurodivergent students). The AI Act treats this as categorically unacceptable regardless of purported benefits.
:::
:::

**Art. 5(1)(g): Biometric Categorization**

Using biometric data to infer race, political opinions, trade union membership, religious beliefs, sex life, or sexual orientation—except for labeling lawfully acquired biometric datasets.

**What this prohibits:** Deploying facial analysis to infer ethnicity for targeted advertising. Using voice analysis to detect sexual orientation for insurance pricing.

**Why it matters:** Such categorization enables automated discrimination at scale. Even if accurate (and these systems often aren't), inferring sensitive attributes without consent violates dignity and autonomy.

**Art. 5(1)(h): Real-Time Remote Biometric Identification**

Using real-time remote biometric identification systems in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement, except under tightly defined conditions (serious crimes, imminent threats, search for missing persons) with judicial authorization.

This is the "facial recognition in public spaces" prohibition. Narrow exceptions exist for severe threats, but routine surveillance is banned.

### High-Risk AI Systems: Art. 6 and Annex III

Not all AI is prohibited—but certain applications face stringent requirements.

**Art. 6:** An AI system is high-risk if:
1. It's listed in Annex III, OR
2. It's a safety component of a product covered by EU harmonization legislation (e.g., medical devices, automotive systems)

**Annex III categories include:**
- Biometric identification and categorization of persons
- Management/operation of critical infrastructure (transport, energy, water)
- Education and vocational training (access, assessment, monitoring)
- Employment (recruitment, task allocation, promotion, termination, monitoring)
- Access to essential services (creditworthiness, insurance pricing, emergency services)
- Law enforcement (individual risk assessment, polygraphs, crime analytics)
- Migration and border control
- Administration of justice and democratic processes

**Key insight:** If your AI system falls into any Annex III category, you face comprehensive compliance obligations *before* placing it on the market.

### Requirements for High-Risk Systems: Art. 8-15

High-risk AI systems must satisfy these mandatory requirements:

**Art. 8: Risk Management System**

Implement a continuous, iterative process to identify, assess, mitigate, and monitor risks throughout the system lifecycle. This isn't a one-time assessment—it's ongoing governance.

**Art. 10: Data Governance**

Training, validation, and testing datasets must be:
- **Relevant:** Appropriate for the intended purpose
- **Representative:** Covering the range of situations/populations the system will encounter
- **To the best extent possible, free from errors** and complete
- **Statistically appropriate properties** for the task

::: {.details}
#### What "Representative" Means in Practice

Representative data isn't merely "large" data. A facial recognition system trained on 10 million images of white faces isn't representative if deployed on diverse populations.

**Requirements:**
- Demographic representation matching deployment context
- Coverage of edge cases and minorities
- Geographic, cultural, and linguistic diversity where relevant
- Explicit documentation of data characteristics and limitations

If your system will be used in hospitals, training data must include hospital environments. If it affects people with disabilities, disabled people must appear in training data with sufficient frequency to achieve comparable accuracy.

**The AI Act codifies what the ethics module taught:** Technical performance on majority groups doesn't satisfy legal obligations when minorities experience significantly worse outcomes.
:::

**Art. 11: Technical Documentation**

Maintain documentation demonstrating compliance with all requirements. This includes:
- System design and architecture
- Data provenance and characteristics
- Training methodology
- Testing results and performance metrics
- Risk assessments
- Human oversight mechanisms

**Art. 13: Transparency and Information Provision**

Design systems so that users can interpret outputs and use them appropriately. Provide instructions that are:
- Concise
- Complete
- Correct
- Clear
- User-friendly

**Art. 14: Human Oversight**

Design systems enabling human oversight to prevent or minimize risks. Humans must be able to:
- Fully understand system capacities and limitations
- Remain aware of automation bias
- Correctly interpret outputs
- Decide not to use the system
- Intervene or interrupt operation
- **Override** system decisions

::: {.flip-card}
#### Automation Bias

The tendency to favor suggestions from automated systems, even when those suggestions are incorrect. Humans are more likely to accept algorithmic outputs uncritically—precisely when critical evaluation matters most.
:::

**Critical point:** Human oversight isn't satisfied by placing a human "in the loop" who rubber-stamps algorithmic decisions. The human must have genuine capacity to understand, question, and override—and the organizational context must permit them to do so without penalty.

**Art. 15: Accuracy, Robustness, Cybersecurity**

Systems must achieve appropriate levels of accuracy and be robust against errors, faults, and manipulation. They must be resilient to cyberattacks.

### Obligations of Providers and Deployers

**Providers** (entities placing AI systems on the market) bear primary responsibility for compliance. They must:
- Ensure systems meet requirements before market placement
- Implement quality management systems
- Conduct conformity assessments
- Register high-risk systems in EU database
- Implement post-market monitoring

**Deployers** (entities using AI systems under their authority) must:
- Comply with instructions for use
- Ensure human oversight
- Monitor operation for risks
- Inform providers of serious incidents
- Conduct fundamental rights impact assessments (for high-risk systems in certain domains)

**Shared responsibility:** If you're developing a custom AI system for an organization, you may be the provider. If the organization uses your system, they're the deployer. Contractual clarity on responsibilities is essential.

### Transparency Obligations: Art. 50

Even AI systems not classified as high-risk face transparency requirements if they:
- Interact with humans (chatbots, virtual assistants)
- Generate synthetic content (deepfakes, AI-generated text/images/audio)
- Are used for emotion recognition or biometric categorization (outside prohibited contexts)

**Requirement:** Inform individuals that they're interacting with AI or that content is AI-generated, unless obvious from context.

**Why this matters:** People have the right to know when they're engaging with machines rather than humans, and when content is synthetic rather than authentic. Deception—even for benign purposes—undermines trust and autonomy.

---

## Integrating GDPR and AI Act

These regulations interact. An AI system processing personal data must comply with **both**.

**Example:** A high-risk recruitment AI system must:
- Satisfy GDPR requirements (legal basis for processing, transparency, data minimization, etc.)
- Satisfy AI Act requirements (risk management, data governance, human oversight, etc.)
- Respect Art. 22 GDPR (no solely automated decisions with significant effects without safeguards)
- Not constitute prohibited practices under Art. 5 AI Act

**Common compliance failures:**
- Claiming "legitimate interest" under GDPR while deploying a system that constitutes prohibited social scoring under the AI Act
- Implementing Art. 14 AI Act human oversight but failing to provide Art. 22 GDPR rights (human review, contestation)
- Achieving Art. 10 AI Act data quality requirements but violating GDPR data minimization by training on excessive personal data

**Best practice:** Integrated compliance assessment addressing both frameworks simultaneously.

---

## What This Means for Developers

You might object: "These regulations make AI development impossible. The requirements are too strict. Innovation will suffer."

Consider this reframing: Legal frameworks define minimum standards for **responsible** development. If your system cannot be built while respecting fundamental rights, perhaps it shouldn't be built.

The AI Act doesn't ban AI—it bans certain harmful practices and demands safeguards for risky applications. Countless AI systems fall outside high-risk categories entirely. Among those that are high-risk, compliance is achievable if you design with legal requirements from the beginning rather than treating them as afterthoughts.

**Practical strategies:**

**1. Conduct early legal classification**

Before investing heavily in development, determine:
- Does your system qualify as "AI" under Art. 3(1)?
- Does it process personal data (triggering GDPR)?
- Does it fall into a prohibited category (Art. 5 AI Act)?
- Does it qualify as high-risk (Annex III)?

Early classification prevents building systems you cannot legally deploy.

**2. Implement privacy by design and by default**

GDPR Art. 25 requires embedding data protection into system design. Concretely:
- Minimize data collection to what's strictly necessary
- Implement pseudonymization/anonymization where possible
- Design for data subject rights (access, deletion, portability)
- Default to privacy-protective settings

**3. Document everything**

Both regulations demand comprehensive documentation. Maintain records of:
- Design decisions and rationale
- Data sources and characteristics
- Training and testing procedures
- Risk assessments and mitigation measures
- Changes and updates

If you cannot document compliance, you are non-compliant.

**4. Build diverse teams**

Homogeneous teams produce systems with blind spots. Legal compliance—particularly around bias and fairness—requires perspectives from affected communities.

**5. Engage legal expertise early**

Waiting until deployment to consult lawyers is too late. Legal review should occur at:
- Concept stage (feasibility assessment)
- Design stage (requirement specification)
- Development stage (ongoing compliance verification)
- Deployment stage (final assessment)

**6. Recognize limits**

Some problems don't have technical solutions. If your system cannot achieve representative data, cannot provide meaningful human oversight, or inevitably produces discriminatory outcomes, the legally compliant choice is to **not deploy it**.

---

## Key Takeaways

**1. Personal data protection is a fundamental right, not a preference.**

GDPR doesn't merely regulate data markets—it recognizes informational privacy as essential to human dignity. AI systems processing personal data must respect this foundation.

**2. Legal bases aren't loopholes.**

You cannot bypass GDPR by claiming data is "public," processing is "necessary," or individuals "consented" through buried terms of service. Each legal basis has specific requirements that must be genuinely satisfied.

**3. Automated decisions require human safeguards.**

Art. 22 GDPR grants rights against solely automated consequential decisions. Art. 14 AI Act requires human oversight for high-risk systems. Both demand *meaningful* human involvement—not performative review.

**4. Some AI practices are categorically prohibited.**

The AI Act establishes red lines: manipulative systems, social scoring, workplace emotion recognition, predictive policing based solely on profiling. No amount of technical sophistication makes these permissible.

**5. High-risk classification triggers comprehensive obligations.**

If your system falls under Annex III, compliance isn't optional. Risk management, data governance, documentation, transparency, and human oversight are mandatory *before* market placement.

**6. Representative data is a legal requirement, not an aspiration.**

Art. 10 AI Act demands training data be representative and, to the best extent possible, free from errors. Deploying systems with known disparate impacts on minorities violates this requirement.

**7. Transparency serves accountability.**

Both GDPR (Art. 13-15) and the AI Act (Art. 13, 50) mandate transparency about data processing and algorithmic decision-making. Trade secrecy does not override individual rights to understand and challenge consequential decisions.

**8. Compliance is iterative, not one-time.**

Risk management (Art. 8 AI Act) and accountability (Art. 5(2) GDPR) require continuous monitoring and updating. Systems lawful at deployment may become non-compliant if context shifts or risks materialize.

**9. Enforcement is real and growing.**

GDPR fines reach hundreds of millions of euros. AI Act sanctions match GDPR levels (up to €35 million or 7% of global turnover for prohibited practices violations). Regulatory authorities are increasingly sophisticated about AI-specific risks.

**10. Legal compliance enables ethical practice.**

These regulations codify principles that responsible developers should embrace regardless of legal obligation: respect for autonomy, fairness, transparency, accountability. Law provides a floor, not a ceiling.

---

## Reflection: Your Legal Responsibility

::: {.flip-card}
#### For Developers and Engineers

**Front:** What legal obligations do you bear when building AI systems? How does technical knowledge intersect with legal compliance?

**Back:**

If you're functioning as a **controller** (determining purposes/means of processing), you bear primary legal responsibility under GDPR. If you're developing a high-risk AI system, you're the **provider** under the AI Act—compliance obligations rest with you.

"I'm just following specifications" isn't a defense. If you recognize that system requirements violate GDPR or the AI Act, you have professional responsibility to raise concerns.

**Your unique contribution:** Technical expertise enables you to identify when systems *cannot* comply—when representative data is unavailable, when meaningful human oversight is technically infeasible, when accuracy requirements cannot be met. Legal compliance depends on honest technical assessment.

**Most importantly:** You have the power to say no to building systems that violate legal requirements or fundamental rights. Exercise that power.
:::

::: {.flip-card}
#### For Policy and Social Science Students

**Front:** How do legal frameworks shape AI development? What gaps remain?

**Back:**

Legal frameworks establish boundaries, but cannot substitute for ethical judgment. The AI Act permits many practices that remain ethically questionable (predictive policing with sufficient safeguards, emotion recognition for medical purposes, high-risk employment systems if requirements are met).

**Your role:** Advocate for stronger protections. Participate in regulatory processes. Monitor enforcement. Challenge systems that technically comply but cause harm.

You bring perspectives that technologists and lawyers often miss: understanding of power dynamics, recognition of structural discrimination, awareness of lived experiences under algorithmic governance.

**Critical questions only you can answer:** Are the protected categories (Annex III) comprehensive enough? Do transparency requirements genuinely enable accountability? Can human oversight function effectively given organizational pressures? Does enforcement prioritize affected communities' concerns?

Legal frameworks evolve through advocacy. Your voice shapes that evolution.
:::
